# Builders

## Functions

### check

```ts
export declare function check<T>(test: (value: T) => CheckAnswer, issue?: IssueInput | Message): Check<T>;
export declare function check<T>(test: (value: T) => CheckAnswer | PromiseLike<CheckAnswer>, issue?: IssueInput | Message): AsyncCheck<T>;
```

Makes a check from a test of a typed value, for a rule a validator's options do not express.

Give it to a validator after its options. It runs once the value has its type and has passed the validator's options, such as `min` and `max`: for an object, once every property has passed, so it can compare them. A test that returns a promise makes an [`AsyncCheck`](index.md#asynccheck), and the validator given it asynchronous.

A test that has more to say than yes or no returns the issues it found, each as `fail` takes one, and an empty list for a value that passes. Their paths are relative to the value the check was given.

A validator takes no other function as a check: what runs a check comes with `check`, so a schema without one carries none of it.

**Parameters**

- `test` — Returns `true` when the value is acceptable and `false` when it is not, or the issues it found.
- `issue` — What to report when the test returns `false`: an issue, or a message, text or a function of the issue, as a built-in check takes. Defaults to code `"custom"` at the value's own location. Its message also words the issues of a list that have none.

**Type parameters**

- `T` — The type of the value it checks.

**Returns** — A check that reports the issue when `test` returns `false`, or the issues it returns.

**Throws** — `TypeError` — When `test` is not a function, or `issue` is neither a message nor an issue: an object that is not a list, whose `code` and `message` are text when given, and whose `path` is a list. From the returned check, when `test` returns neither a boolean nor a list of issues.

**Example**

```ts
const even = check((n: number) => n % 2 === 0, "Must be even");
number({ int: true }, even);

const signup = object(
  { password: string({ min: 8 }), confirm: string() },
  check((data) => data.password === data.confirm, { path: ["confirm"], message: "Passwords must match" }),
);

const range = check((data: { from: number; to: number }) =>
  data.from <= data.to ? [] : [{ code: "range", path: ["from"] }, { code: "range", path: ["to"] }],
);
```

### checkFields

```ts
export declare function checkFields<T extends object, const TKey extends keyof T & string>(keys: readonly TKey[], test: (value: Pick<T, TKey>) => boolean, issue?: IssueInput | Message): Check<T>;
export declare function checkFields<T extends object, const TKey extends keyof T & string>(keys: readonly TKey[], test: (value: Pick<T, TKey>) => boolean | PromiseLike<boolean>, issue?: IssueInput | Message): AsyncCheck<T>;
```

Makes a check of an object that needs only some of its properties, and so does not wait for the others: given to `object` or `objectLike`, it runs as soon as every property it names has passed, whatever the rest did.

A check made by `check` is given the whole object, so it runs once every property has passed, and a form shows "Passwords must match" only after every other field is valid. This one is given an object of the named properties alone, typed so, and reports with the issues of the properties that failed.

It takes the issue to report as `check` does: a message, a function that words the issue, or an issue with its own `code`, `path`, `params` and `message`. A property named here that the object does not have is a `TypeError` when the object is created. Given to any other validator it is a check like any other, run once the value has passed.

**Parameters**

- `keys` — The properties the test needs, each of which the object has.
- `test` — Returns whether an object of those properties is acceptable.
- `issue` — The message, or the issue to report. Defaults to the code `custom` at the object itself.

**Type parameters**

- `T` — The type of the object.
- `TKey` — The properties the test reads.

**Returns** — A check for an object with those properties.

**Throws** — `TypeError` — When `keys` is not a list of property names or is empty, `test` is not a function, or `issue` is not a message or an issue object.

**Example**

```ts
const signup = object(
  { name: string({ min: 2 }), password: string({ min: 12 }), confirm: string() },
  checkFields(["password", "confirm"], (data) => data.password === data.confirm, {
    path: ["confirm"],
    message: "Passwords must match",
  }),
);
signup({ name: "", password: "correct horse battery", confirm: "nope" });
// fails with the issue of `name` and "Passwords must match" at `confirm`
```

### format

```ts
export declare function format(name: string, test: (text: string) => boolean): Factory<string, MessageOptions>;
```

Makes the factory of a validator for a string format, which behaves exactly as `email()` or `uuid()` do.

A value that is not a string fails with `invalid_type`, and a string the test rejects with `invalid_format` and `params.format` set to `name`. An accepted string is returned as written. The validators it makes take a `message` option and checks.

**Parameters**

- `name` — The name of the format, for the issue. Treat it as part of the format's contract.
- `test` — Returns `true` for a string of the format.

**Returns** — The factory of the validator.

**Throws** — `TypeError` — When `name` is not text or `test` is not a function, and, from the validator, when `test` returns a promise, which would accept every value: a rule that waits is a check.

**Example**

```ts
const slug = format("slug", (text) => /^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$/.test(text));
slug()("hello-world"); // { ok: true, value: "hello-world" }
slug({ message: "Use lowercase words and hyphens" })("Hello World"); // { ok: false, ... }
```

### guard

```ts
export declare function guard<T>(expected: string, accepts: (input: unknown) => input is T): Factory<T, MessageOptions>;
```

Makes the factory of a validator for any type, from a type guard.

A value the guard rejects fails with `invalid_type` and `params.expected` set to `expected`. The validators it makes take a `message` option and checks, as every built-in one does.

**Parameters**

- `expected` — The name of the type, for the issue.
- `accepts` — Returns `true` for a value of the type.

**Type parameters**

- `T` — The type the guard accepts.

**Returns** — The factory of the validator.

**Throws** — `TypeError` — When `expected` is not text or `accepts` is not a function, and, from the validator, when `accepts` returns a promise, which would accept every value: a rule that waits is a check.

**Example**

```ts
const file = guard("File", (input): input is File => input instanceof File);
const upload = object({ avatar: file({ message: "Choose an image" }) });
```

### validator

```ts
export declare function validator<TReturn extends Validated, TInput = unknown>(validate: ((input: unknown) => TReturn) & {
    readonly "~types"?: {
        readonly input: TInput;
    };
}): [Extract<TReturn, PromiseLike<unknown>>] extends [never] ? Schema<ValidatedValue<TReturn>, TInput> : AsyncSchema<ValidatedValue<TReturn>, TInput>;
```

Makes a validator from a function written by hand, for a value no factory or builder of this package describes.

The function is given the input and returns `pass(value)` or `fail(issue)`, or a promise of one, which makes the validator asynchronous. The paths of its issues are relative to the value it was given, and a composer places them. A validator it calls in turn is part of the same validation.

A composer takes no other function as a validator: what calls a function written by hand, and waits for it, comes with `validator`, so a schema without one carries none of it.

**Parameters**

- `validate` — Returns the result for an input.

**Type parameters**

- `TReturn` — What the function returns, which says the type of the value and whether it waits.
- `TInput` — The type of input that can pass, read from a function typed as a validator and `unknown` otherwise.

**Returns** — A validator that gives what `validate` returns, asynchronous when `validate` may return a promise.

**Throws** — `TypeError` — When `validate` is not a function. From the returned validator, when `validate` returns something that is not a result, a failure without issues, or an issue `fail()` would refuse: one that is not an object, with a `code` or `message` that is not text, or a `path` that is not a list of keys and indexes.

**Example**

```ts
const even = validator((input) =>
  typeof input === "number" && input % 2 === 0 ? pass(input) : fail({ code: "odd" }),
);
even(4); // { ok: true, value: 4 }
object({ count: even })({ count: 3 }); // { ok: false, ... }, code "odd" at ["count"]
```

The type of the value is read from what the function returns, so a function that returns `pass(input)` for a `number` makes a validator of `number`. To say it, type what the function returns, as in `(input): ValidationResult<User> => ...`.

## Type aliases

### CheckAnswer

```ts
export type CheckAnswer = boolean | readonly IssueInput[];
```

What the test of a check answers: whether the value is acceptable, or the issues it found, none for a value that is.

### Validated

```ts
export type Validated = ValidationResult<unknown> | PromiseLike<ValidationResult<unknown>>;
```

What a function written by hand returns: a result, or a promise of one.

### ValidatedValue

```ts
export type ValidatedValue<TReturn> = Extract<Awaited<TReturn>, {
    ok: true;
    value: unknown;
}>["value"];
```

The type of the value in the results `TReturn` holds.
